NTSB:20240912195112.s: Alaska Airlines flight 369 rejected takeoff on runway 13 at Nashville after Southwest Airlines flight 2029 crossed the runway at taxiway T5. No injuries or damage occurred, though the Alaska aircraft later deflated all four main landing gear tires while waiting for a gate.

NTSB:20240912195113.n: The pilot reported that during a go-around, the right-wing leading-edge slat retracted to the stowed position, and the airplane rolled to the right. The pilot attempted to correct with opposite aileron; however, the airplane continued the right roll and impacted the ground. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings, fuselage, and the empennage. According to the airplane kit manufacturer, the wing leading-edge slats are self-deploying and self-stowing. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20240912195113.s: During a go-around, the pilot reported the right-wing leading-edge slat retracted, causing an uncontrollable right roll and ground impact. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the wings, fuselage, and empennage, with no preaccident mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20240913195116.n: The pilot was conducting a personal flight when during cruise descent the engine began to sputter and suddenly lost power. He moved the throttle to full-forward and increased the mixture to full-rich, but the engine resumed operation only 5 to 10 seconds before it lost power a second time. The pilot reported that the airplane was at low altitude that required an immediate forced landing into a nearby cornfield. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mounts, fuselage structure, and right wing. Examination of the airplane fuel system and the engine revealed no evidence of a preimpact mechanical malfunction. There was ample fuel recovered from the fuel tanks at the accident site, and there was no evidence of any water or particulate contamination of the fuel system. The weather conditions at the time of the accident were in the range of susceptibility for the formation of serious carburetor icing at glide engine power. According to a Federal Aviation Administration Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin, pilots should use carburetor heat while in weather conditions where carburetor icing is probable. When interviewed, the pilot acknowledged that he did not review a carburetor icing chart before the flight. However, he stipulated that he applied carburetor heat after the engine began sputtering. Based on the available information, the loss of engine power was likely due to carburetor ice accumulation. Additionally, the low altitude at which the loss of engine power occurred significantly reduced the amount of time available to the pilot to troubleshoot and restore engine power before the forced landing.
NTSB:20240913195116.s: During a personal flight's cruise descent, the pilot experienced engine power loss likely caused by carburetor ice, leading to a forced landing in a cornfield. The aircraft sustained substantial damage, and the low altitude limited time to troubleshoot before impact.

NTSB:20240913195117.n: The pilot estimated that he touched down about 100 ft past the numbers while landing. He attempted to decelerate, keeping constant pressure on the brakes. The pilot stated that the brakes were not working until he approached the end of the runway, at which point the brakes "slowly got responsive." The pilot reported that a go-around was possible and that it was a "shock" that he couldn' t stop the airplane. He reported that the approach and landing was made with the flaps set to "APP." The airplane exited the paved surface of the runway and impacted a runway end identifier light, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage. A postaccident examination of the brake system revealed no anomalies that would have precluded normal operation, and a postaccident runway inspection by the airport manager revealed visible tire skid marks leading off the end of the runway. An aircraft performance study using ADS-B and engine control unit (ECU) data concluded that the airplane touched down at 92 kts calibrated airspeed (KCAS), 6 kts faster than the 86-kt VREF speed calculated from the airplane flight manual. The airplane's weight on wheels sensors indicated that the airplane was not fully on the ground until 2,136 ft past the runway threshold. The airplane landed in a 6.3 kt tailwind that would have increased landing distance by 21%. Considering all factors, the study concluded that insufficient runway remained after the touchdown for the airplane to stop. Additionally, the study concluded that had the pilot used the LDG flap setting, there would have been sufficient runway remaining.
NTSB:20240913195117.s: The pilot landed a tailwind-affected aircraft with APP flaps at excessive speed, resulting in a runway overrun and fuselage damage after brakes became responsive late. Investigation concluded insufficient runway remained due to high touchdown speed and flap setting, though post-accident brake checks found no anomalies.

NTSB:20240913195118.n: The pilot of a tailwheel equipped airplane reported he was attempting to depart from a remote 600ft-long airstrip. The pilot said just after the airplane lifted off the ground, it encountered windshear and did not gain sufficient altitude to clear rising terrain at the end of the airstrip. The airplane's tailwheel impacted terrain, and the airplane veered to the left. Subsequently, the airplane impacted terrain again and came to rest upright. The right wing and fuselage sustained substantial damage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20240913195118.s: The pilot of a tailwheel-equipped airplane encountered windshear immediately after departing a 600ft remote airstrip, preventing sufficient altitude gain to clear rising terrain. The aircraft's tailwheel and fuselage struck the ground, causing substantial damage, though the pilot reported no pre-accident mechanical failures.

NTSB:20240913195119.n: On September 13, 2024, about 0803 Alaska daylight time (AKDT), a Champion (Citabria) 7GCBC, N8CK, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ninilchik, Alaska. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to a family member of both occupants, the pilot and passenger departed Lowell Field Airport (00AK), Happy Valley, Alaska about 0700 to conduct a moose spotting flight. About 0745, a witness, located about 4.5 miles southwest of the accident site, reported seeing the accident airplane flying low overhead, following an off-roading trail, at an altitude between 100-200 ft above ground level (agl) with a crab angle of about 10°. The witness reported that, after passing overhead, the accident airplane flew about 500 ft east of his location, circled a group of four moose that were standing in an open field, then proceeded to fly northbound and out of view. (See figure 1) Figure 1: Chart depicting witness location relative to the accident site About 0803, the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center (RCC) received a 406 Mhz emergency locator transmitter (ELT) signal assigned to the accident airplane from a location Southwest of Tustumena Lake. The RCC contacted the Federal Aviation Administration Kenai Flight Service Station, who routed an airplane over the location of the ELT signal to confirm the presence of a downed airplane. The RCC simultaneously dispatched search and rescue personnel to the accident site. (See figure 2) Figure 2: Aerial view of the accident site (NTSB Photo) The airplane came to rest about seven miles southwest of Tustumena Lake in an area of hilly, sparsely forested, tundra-covered terrain. The wreckage exhibited signatures consistent with a high angle, nose down impact. (See figure 3) Figure 3: View of the accident at accident site (NTSB Photo) All the major structures and components of the airplane were accounted for at the accident site. The engine was partially burrowed into the soft, tundra-covered terrain, leaving only the top deck of the engine visible. The aft section of the fuselage protruded upwards from the point of impact at about a 50° angle with the empennage suspended about 12 ft above the ground. The outboard section of the right wing exhibited impact damage. The inboard, forward section of the left wing exhibited compression damage. The aft section of the fuselage exhibited lateral deformation in the direction of the right wing. No preimpact anomalies were observed with the flight control system at the wreckage site. The wreckage will be recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20240913195119.s: A pilot and passenger were fatally injured when their Champion 7GCBC, N8CK, crashed near Ninilchik, Alaska, during a Part 91 moose spotting flight. The aircraft sustained substantial damage in a high-angle, nose-down impact after being observed flying low with a crab angle.

NTSB:20240914195120.n: The pilot departed for his first flight in an experimental home-built airplane. Witnesses stated that the engine did not sound like it was producing full power during the takeoff. After the airplane was airborne, one witness saw the airplane's nose come down and the airplane made a slight left bank to line up with a road before the witness lost sight of the airplane. The airplane impacted a road, that was surrounded by trees, in a near-vertical, nose-down attitude and a postimpact fire began. There was tree debris in the area immediately surrounding the wreckage, there were also branches and debris slightly further from the airplane. Postaccident examination revealed that the fuel supply hose from the carburetor to the gascolator was not the correct size. The braided steel hose was too small and was observed to have a kink that likely restricted fuel flow. Postaccident examination of the wreckage found no evidence of any other preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airframe or engine, other than the fuel line, that would have precluded normal operation. Because of the fuel line's size and improper installation, the carburetor was likely not able to supply enough fuel to the engine at full power during the takeoff. Based on the tree debris surrounding the accident site, it is likely that while maneuvering to land on the road, the airplane impacted trees resulting in a loss of control and impact with the road.
NTSB:20240914195120.s: The pilot of an experimental home-built airplane crashed during takeoff after a kinked, undersized fuel hose restricted engine power. The aircraft struck trees while maneuvering toward a road, resulting in a nose-down impact and postimpact fire.

NTSB:20240916195122.n: The pilot reported he was inbound to land and was waiting for a break in chatter on the radio to contact the air traffic control tower. He was about 7 miles from the airport, and about 1,050 ft mean sea level when he encountered wake turbulence presumably from a Boeing 747 inbound to an adjacent runway. He stated the airplane violently dropped and he struck his head on the ceiling. He was able to maintain control of the airplane and land uneventfully. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing. The pilot reported there were no mechanical malfunctions or anomalies with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20240916195122.s: A pilot inbound to land at 1,050 feet encountered wake turbulence from a Boeing 747, causing the aircraft to drop violently and strike his head. Although he maintained control and landed uneventfully, the airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing with no mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20240916195123.n: On September 15, 2024, about 2204 Alaska daylight time, a Cessna 207 airplane, N90193, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near St. Mary’s, Alaska. The pilot and three passengers were fatally injured. The flight was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. According to the operator, Yute Commuter Service, the airplane was reportedly being used by two employees for a personal flight at the time of the accident. Management personnel reported that the accident airplane was currently only being used for Part 91 operations since the engine had exceeded the manufacturers time before overhaul requirement. These Part 91 operations included company flight training and repositioning flights. The accident pilot, who was the assistant chief pilot for the operator, along with another company pilot, a former pilot for the operator, and a fourth passenger, intended to fly from Bethel Airport (BET), Bethel, Alaska, to St. Mary’s Airport (KSM), St. Mary’s, Alaska, for a moose hunt. According to the flight tracking service used by the operator, the airplane departed BET about 2108 and proceeded to the northwest to KSM between 500 and 800 ft above ground level (agl). At 2159, the airplane was about 4 nautical miles southeast of the KSM airport and about 180 ft agl over the Yukon River. The airplane continued north toward the airport, overflew the west side of runway 6/24, then maneuvered to the west of the airport. The airplane then made a left 180° turn and overflew runway 6/24 about 200 ft agl. The airplane turned right and proceeded south, then made a steep right descending turn toward the ground. The final recorded point was above the accident site (See figure 1). Figure 1. Accident flight track near St. Mary’s Airport overlaid on Google Earth. According to the operator, the accident airplane was equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS–B), which provides aircraft position information via satellite navigation or other sensors and periodically broadcasts it, enabling the aircraft to be tracked. The information can be received by air traffic control ground stations as a replacement for secondary surveillance radar, as no interrogation signal is needed from the ground. However, no ADS-B data was received from the accident airplane, during the accident flight. According to archived Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) air traffic control radio communications, the accident pilot contacted the Anchorage Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) controller on-duty when the airplane was about 10 miles southwest of KSM and requested a special visual flight rules (SVFR) clearance to enter the KSM airport environment. The ARTCC controller subsequently provided the current weather conditions and issued the pilot a SVFR clearance. At 2155, the ARTCC controller instructed the pilot to change to the KSM airport advisory frequency and to report canceling the SVFR clearance once on the ground at KSM. At 2235, about 25 minutes after the facility-estimated arrival time at the airport, the controller attempted to contact the airplane with no response. An alert notice (ALNOT) was issued at 2300 for the overdue airplane. At 2156, KSM automated weather reported wind from 280° at 13 knots, visibility 2 1/2 miles with light rain and mist, ceiling overcast at 300 ft agl, temperature and dew point 8° Celsius (C) (46°F), altimeter setting 29.30 inches of mercury. Remarks: automated system with a precipitation discriminator, visibility 1 mile variable 5 miles, rain began at 2103 AKDT, hourly precipitation 0.01 inches, 6-hour rainfall 0.7 inches, temperature 7.8°C, dew point 7.8°C, 6-hour maximum temperature 8.9C, 6-hour minimum temperature 7.8C, 3-hour pressure tendency risen 3.7-hPa. The sunset at KSM occurred at 2110 and civil twilight ended and 2155. On the day of the accident, another company airplane departed BET on a scheduled 14 CFR Part 135 flight to KSM. According to the flight track data, the airplane arrived near KSM at 2128 and departed the area about 2135 without landing, and then returned to Bethel. The pilot of the airplane reported that weather conditions along the flight route to KSM were “going up and down a lot,” and the visibility went up to 10 miles at one point, but as they got closer to KSM, it was about 1 ¼ miles. Due to the weather, he turned around to return to Bethel, but then KSM went back up to 4 miles visibility. He turned back to KSM and requested a SVFR clearance from ARTCC. After receiving the clearance, the KSM visibility went down to ½ mile. As he approached KSM, he could see the hills surrounding the airport and Pitkas Point but could not see the runway environment; KSM appeared completely “fogged in,” so he canceled the SVFR approach and returned to BET. He added that the long runway 17/35 was closed at the time and the lights on runway 6/24 (the shorter runway) were inoperative. Since the wind was favoring runway 24, he had planned to land on the shorter runway. During his first attempt to land at KSM, he didn’t see any runways or the airport at all. During the approach, he could only see the surrounding hills and Pitkas Point, but not the runways or lights. He did attempt to activate the pilot-controlled runway lights for runway 17/35, but due to the reduced visibility he never saw the lights, the airport beacon, or any part of the runway environment at all. A senior National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigator-in-charge (IIC), along with an FAA aviation airworthiness inspector, and an air safety investigator from Textron Aviation, responded to the accident site and examined the airplane wreckage on September 18. During the detailed on-scene examination, the investigative team documented the wreckage before recovery efforts began. The NTSB on-scene wreckage examination revealed that the airplane impacted rising terrain in a right wing low and nose low attitude on a northwest heading. The highly fragmented debris path was about 150 ft long and contained all major components of the airplane (See figure 2). Figure 2. A view of the airplane wreckage at the accident site facing north (Courtesy of FAA). The airplane wreckage was recovered for the accident site and transported to Wasilla, Alaska, and a detailed NTSB examination is pending.
NTSB:20240916195123.s: The assistant chief pilot of a Cessna 207 was fatally injured with three passengers when the aircraft impacted terrain near St. Mary's, Alaska, during a night personal flight. The accident occurred in low visibility and overcast conditions after the pilot maneuvered near the airport following a special VFR clearance.

NTSB:20240916195125.n: The pilot had flown the airplane on two separate uneventful flights earlier that day and was departing on another flight around the airport traffic pattern with two passengers when the engine lost power during takeoff. The pilot landed fast on the remaining portion of the runway. With the throttle still applied, engine power resumed, causing the airplane to become airborne again. The engine then lost power again when the airplane was beyond the departure end of the runway, causing the pilot to land on grass. The airplane then rolled along terrain before coming to rest adjacent to a building on the airport property, with substantial damage to the airplane’s right wing. Postaccident examination of the engine, engine controls including carburetor heat, fuel supply, fuel vent, air induction, exhaust, and ignition systems revealed no evidence of preimpact failure or malfunction that would have precluded normal operation. Although operational testing of the carburetor revealed no discrepancies with the accelerator pump, mixture control, or performance of the main circuit, subsequent testing revealed restriction of the float caused by the float pontoons contacting the interior walls of the test bowl. Further, the float hinge was worn 0.002 inches beyond specified limits. Although the carburetor had been in service for more than 43 years, it was considered an on-condition item for Part 91 operators and, as such, was not subject to a set overhaul period based on calendar or operational time. Based on the results of the postaccident examination, the carburetor’s undetected worn internal parts likely restricted movement of the float, preventing fuel from entering the float bowl as fuel was consumed during takeoff, which resulted in fuel starvation. Additionally, had the pilot reduced throttle when performing the first forced landing on the remaining portion of the runway, the flight duration would have been shortened, lessening the chance for airplane damage.
NTSB:20240916195125.s: The pilot experienced engine power loss during takeoff due to fuel starvation caused by a worn carburetor float hinge restricting fuel flow. The aircraft sustained substantial right wing damage after landing on grass beyond the runway following a second power loss.

NTSB:20240916195126.n: The pilot of the helicopter was performing external lift operations when he noticed an “intermittent and unusual vibration.” The pilot performed a precautionary landing, and a postflight inspection of the main rotor system revealed a crack in one main rotor blade, which constituted substantial damage to the helicopter. Postaccident examination of the main rotor blade revealed that a large crack extended from the leading edge spar on the lower surface to the middle of the main rotor blade along the doubler leading edge on the upper surface of the blade. There was an area of chipped paint adjacent to the crack at the outboard tip of the root fitting on the lower side of the blade. After sectioning, the large crack was mechanically exposed and examined stereoscopically. Feathery features consistent with fatigue were observed on the lower side fracture surfaces of the doubler, skin, and spar. Scanning electron microscope examination revealed numerous ratchet marks at the doubler-skin and skin-spar interfaces emanating at the outboard sides of both layers, consistent with multiple initiation fatigue starting from the outboard side. Dark-colored deposits were observed on the spar fracture surface at the tip and on the adjacent skin fracture surface due to the rubbing of mating fracture surfaces. The large size of the crack and the rubbing of the mating fracture surfaces was consistent with fatigue crack growth over an extended period of time. The accident helicopter main rotor blades were subject to an FAA Airworthiness Directive (AD) for regular inspections due to the helicopter’s use for external lift operations. The cracked main rotor blade was installed onto the accident helicopter the month before the accident and had accrued about 67 hours of operation since installation. The operator reported that an inspection in accordance with the AD (AD 2005-21-02) was most recently performed 6 days (12.4 flight hours) before the accident. Maintenance personnel noted no defects during recent inspections. According to the operator, the inboard portion of the main rotor blade was painted gloss white by the operator’s director of maintenance sometime during the month of the accident; however, there were no maintenance records reflecting when or by whom the painting was performed or inspected. It is likely that the fatigue crack occurred sometime between when the main rotor blade was installed onto the helicopter and before the accident flight; however, when the fatigue crack occurred could not be determined. Manufacturer guidance stated that the identification of cracks in main rotor blades requires a careful examination, including the use of supplemental lighting and optical magnification. Whether maintenance personnel performed the inspections with adequate lighting and magnification was not determined. Additionally, it could not be determined whether the fatigue cracking may have been concealed by the recent painting of the main rotor blade.
NTSB:20240916195126.s: The helicopter pilot performing external lift operations executed a precautionary landing after detecting unusual vibration caused by a fatigue crack in a main rotor blade. The blade, installed 67 hours prior and recently painted without records, had a crack missed during a mandatory inspection six days before the accident.

NTSB:20240916195128.n: A high-winged Cessna and low-winged Swift collided in midair while operating in the traffic pattern for the same destination runway. The Cessna had completed a touch-and-go landing and was climbing on the left crosswind leg toward the traffic pattern altitude. The Swift was approaching the airport from the northwest/west on a southeast-bound 45° intercept to the left downwind leg off the traffic pattern. About 17 seconds before the presumed collision time, the Swift pilot transmitted on the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency that he was entering the area on a 45° intercept to the downwind leg. The Cessna pilots subsequently began scanning for the Swift, and the right-seated pilot also checked the traffic display. The Swift was not equipped with ADS-B, no traffic target was displayed in the Cessna, and neither Cessna pilot visually acquired the Swift before impact. The Cessna pilots did not state their position after completing the touch-and-go until after the Swift pilot made a transmission of his position, which was just before impact. If the Cessna pilots had made an earlier position transmission it may have given the Swift pilot an opportunity to make visual contact while approaching the airport. Recorded data from the Cessna, video evidence, and the physical contact signatures on both airplanes were consistent with the Cessna climbing into the Swift from below and aft. Video evidence showed the Swift slightly above the Cessna immediately before the collision. The Cessna’s forward engine and propeller area contacted the lower aft fuselage and tailwheel area of the Swift, resulting in separation of portions of the Swift’s tail section. The relative positions of the airplanes would have placed the Cessna in or near the Swift pilot’s aft blind area. Although the Swift would have been ahead of and slightly above the Cessna during the closing sequence, its limited relative motion against the background likely reduced its visibility to the Cessna pilots. The available evidence was consistent with the pilots of both airplanes not visually acquiring the other airplane in sufficient time to avoid the collision. NTSB:20240916195129.n: The pilot was on final approach to the destination airport. Witnesses observed the airplane flying at a low altitude and heard the engine operating as it maneuvered toward the airport. The airplane appeared to encounter a flock of about 20 birds that rose from a dead tree about 35 ft above the ground. The airplane pitched up and turned left, consistent with the pilot attempting an evasive maneuver to avoid the birds. The airplane collided with a tree and residence. The pilot succumbed to his injuries and could not be interviewed. No bird DNA or feather fragments were detected in samples taken from the airplane. Although no physical evidence of a bird strike was identified, witness observations indicated that the pilot maneuvered to avoid birds that had risen into the airplane's flight path. Witnesses observed the airplane flying at a low altitude as it approached the airport. The pilot likely did not have sufficient altitude to recover from the evasive maneuver before the airplane collided with a tree.
NTSB:20240916195129.s: The pilot on final approach maneuvered to avoid a flock of birds rising from a tree at 35 feet. The aircraft pitched up and turned left but lacked sufficient altitude to recover, resulting in a collision with a tree and residence that killed the pilot.

NTSB:20240917195130.n: The pilot was attempting to land on a 60-ft-wide runway with a 10 to 15 knot left crosswind. He described that he was too high on the approach and made an aggressive right-wing low forward slip to lose altitude. While transitioning to complete the crosswind landing, the pilot misjudged his height above the runway and landed hard, damaging the nose landing gear. The airplane began to veer off the runway and the pilot aborted the landing. On the next landing, when the damaged nose landing gear touched down, the airplane veered off the runway, impacted a trench, and nosed over resulting in substantial damage to the right wing, vertical stabilizer, and rudder. Following the accident, the pilot stated that he should have gone around on the first landing attempt since he was not stabilized on the approach. He also reported there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20240917195130.s: The pilot attempted a crosswind landing on a narrow runway, misjudged altitude during a slip, and damaged the nose gear on a hard touchdown. The aircraft subsequently veered off, impacted a trench, and nosed over, causing substantial damage to the wing and tail.

NTSB:20240917195131.n: The pilot reported that he launched his hot air balloon for a brief solo flight with the intent of practicing maneuvers during calm wind conditions. Shortly after departure, he prepared for landing on a spot about 1/4-mile away that consisted of a flat harvested corn field. During the landing approach, he observed a powerline perpendicular to his final approach and landing target. He initially thought about climbing, but realized the balloon would not react fast enough, so he opened the vent to deflate the envelope and descend. The balloon envelope did not vent quickly enough and the balloon drifted into the powerlines, resulting in electrical arcing until the electrical breaker shut off. The basket settled onto the ground and the balloon envelope remained partially inflated and draped over the powerlines. The arcing resulted in substantial damage to the balloon; 6 cables were severed and there were multiple burn holes in the envelope. The pilot reported that there were no pre impact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the balloon that would have precluded normal operation or performance.
NTSB:20240917195131.s: A solo hot air balloon pilot encountered powerlines during a landing approach in a cornfield. The balloon drifted into the lines because the vent did not open quickly enough, causing electrical arcing that severed cables and burned the envelope.

NTSB:20240917195132.n: The pilot of the tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that after landing, inbound traffic was behind him, and he felt rushed to clear the runway and park the airplane. While taxiing to the ramp, the left main wheel rolled off the taxiway surface and into the grass. The left main landing gear's axle separated from the landing gear leg, the airplane tipped over to the left, and the left wing struck the ground and was substantially damaged. Examination of photographs of the landing gear leg and axle fracture surfaces showed that they displayed indications of fatigue cracking that likely initiated at the toe of the weld that attached the axle to the leg.
NTSB:20240917195132.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane reported that while taxiing to the ramp, the left main wheel left the taxiway, causing the axle to separate from the leg due to fatigue cracking at a weld. The aircraft tipped over, striking the left wing and sustaining substantial damage.

NTSB:20240917195134.n: According to the flight instructor, she was taxiing with a student when she took control and made a left turn to position the airplane between a fence and a fuel station. However, she reported that during the left turn, she misjudged the airplane's clearance and the airplane's left wing struck the fence. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing spar. The flight instructor reported there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20240917195134.s: A flight instructor taxiing a student pilot misjudged clearance during a left turn, causing the airplane's left wing to strike a fence. The incident resulted in substantial damage to the left wing spar, with no preaccident mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20240917195135.n: The pilot was departing from a high-altitude, confined, off-airport site with 2 passengers. The pilot stated that the helicopter was under its maximum gross weight, and he calculated that the helicopter would be able to hover and take off up to about 7,700 ft mean sea level (msl), about 600 ft above the field elevation. During multiple attempts to climb from a hover, the full throttle light on the annunciator panel illuminated; the light would then extinguish when the helicopter altitude was closer to the ground. After some discussion between the pilot and his passengers about the best way to depart the site, the pilot decided to initiate a maximum performance turning takeoff from a hover. Shortly after liftoff, while in a hover, the pilot initiated a climb and the full throttle light illuminated again. The helicopter yawed slightly to the right and continued a slow climbing right turn. The engine and rotor rpms decreased to 95% during the climbing turn. About 2 seconds later, the engine and rotor rpms dropped to about 90%. After turning 270° from its original takeoff heading, the helicopter shallowed its right turn and, after another 2 seconds, the rpms dropped to about 85%. About 4 seconds later, the altimeter showed that the helicopter climbed to about 100 ft above ground level (agl) and increased its right turn rate. The helicopter impacted terrain about 18 seconds later, with the engine and rotor rpms indicating approximately 60%. The pilot thought there might have been issues regarding the fuel that was used during the accident flight. However, the investigation was unable to determine whether the fuel was contaminated or of substandard quality. The manufacturer’s performance charts revealed that the helicopter had in-ground effect hover capability under the conditions of the accident takeoff; however, the helicopter did not have out-of-ground effect hover capability. Furthermore, the pilot knew from multiple attempts to climb from a hover that the helicopter was reaching full throttle and could not continue climbing. Instead of following through with alternative options to safely depart the mountain site, the pilot decided to perform a maximum-power takeoff with limited engine performance. As a result, the helicopter could not maintain the engine and rotor rpms, which resulted in the helicopter settling and subsequently impacting terrain.
NTSB:20240917195135.s: A pilot departed a high-altitude site in a helicopter with two passengers, but the aircraft lost engine and rotor RPMs during a maximum performance takeoff due to insufficient out-of-ground effect hover capability. The pilot ignored full throttle warnings and continued climbing, causing the helicopter to settle and impact terrain.

NTSB:20240917195136.n: The pilot of the multi-engine airplane reported that, during the landing flare as the airplane was about to touch down, an elk ran onto the runway and into the landing path of the airplane. The airplane collided with the animal, the left landing gear collapsed, and the left wing impacted the runway surface. Subsequently, the airplane veered left and exited the left side of the runway before it came to rest. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20240917195136.s: The pilot of a multi-engine airplane reported colliding with an elk during the landing flare, causing the left landing gear to collapse and the left wing to impact the runway. The aircraft veered off the left side of the runway with substantial wing damage, though no pre-accident mechanical failures were reported.

NTSB:20240918195138.n: The flight instructor explained that immediately after the airplane lifted from the runway, a parachutist beneath a fully fully-deployed canopy appeared from above and to the left of the high-winged airplane about 15-20 ft above ground level. The parachutist was aligned to cross the runway from left to right immediately to his front, so he turned right to raise the left wing in hopes of striking the parachute instead of the parachutist. Witnesses described the collision, pieces separating from the airplane, and the parachutist "skidding" across the runway before coming to rest unhurt. The instructor maneuvered the substantially substantially-damaged airplane and landed it successfully with both occupants emerging unhurt. According to the operator of the skydiving activity, the parachutist failed to enter the area surrounding the designated drop zone properly and into the wind, but instead overshot the landing zone in the downwind direction and crossed in front of the departing airplane. In a written statement, the parachutist explained that he was a "student" and that he lacked control of the canopy when he experienced a "sudden change of winds." He stated that the wind "pushed" him in the direction of the departure runway. The parachutist added that because he was a student in a "highly good" training environment, that he would improve his "skills and experience" with more training.
NTSB:20240918195138.s: A flight instructor piloting a high-winged airplane during takeoff collided with a student parachutist who drifted into the departure path due to sudden wind changes. The instructor maneuvered to strike the canopy instead of the person, sustaining substantial damage but landing safely with both occupants and the parachutist unhurt.

NTSB:20240919195143.n: The pilot of the vintage tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that during landing roll, he heard a "pop," followed by an uncommanded right turn. He was unable to correct the turn, and the airplane departed the right side of the runway. The left main landing gear subsequently collapsed on a taxiway, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing. Examination of the wreckage by a Federal Aviation Administration inspector revealed that the tailwheel strut had failed and was in an overextended position, which locked the tailwheel in a right turn. The inspector added that the tailwheel strut had been rebuilt about 15 years and 500 operating hours prior to the accident.
NTSB:20240919195143.s: The pilot of a vintage tailwheel airplane experienced an uncommanded right turn and runway departure during landing due to a failed, overextended tailwheel strut. The strut, rebuilt 15 years prior, locked the wheel, causing the left main gear to collapse and sustain substantial wing damage.

NTSB:20240919195144.n: The pilot reported that during climb out, he noticed a flicker of both the left and right hydraulic flow lights. He thought the airplane was losing hydraulic pressure, so he tried to extend the landing gear before all pressure was lost. Only the left main landing gear position green light illuminated. The hydraulic flow lights then illuminated steadily. He returned to the airport and performed the emergency landing gear extension checklist; however, the right and nose landing gear did not extend, and he landed with only the left main landing gear extended. A postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that a solid hydraulic line connected to the hydraulic filter was fractured and the system contained no hydraulic fluid. It is likely that the fracture of the hydraulic line and the subsequent loss of hydraulic fluid resulted in the partial landing gear extension. A review of the airplane's maintenance records could not determine the age of the hydraulic line or if any maintenance had been performed on the hydraulic line. Postaccident testing of the emergency landing gear extension system revealed that if functioned normally when the activation handle was fully extended. Based on this information, it is likely the pilot did not pull the emergency handle out far enough to activate the system.
NTSB:20240919195144.s: During climb out, a pilot experienced hydraulic fluid loss from a fractured line, causing partial landing gear extension. The aircraft landed on one gear because the pilot likely failed to fully extend the emergency handle, despite the system functioning normally during post-accident testing.

NTSB:20240920195147.n: The helicopter pilot and two medical crewmembers were returning to base at night after completing a patient drop-off at a nearby hospital. The takeoff and cruise portions of the flight were routine. Approaching the landing zone while using night vision goggles, the pilot allowed the helicopter pitch to increase while at a low engine power demand, resulting in the helicopter entering a rapid descent. Recorded flight data showed a late attempt to recover; however, the helicopter struck the ground hard at a descent rate greater than 600 ft/minute, lunged forward, and spun to the right about 220° before coming to a stop. The helicopter was substantially damaged, and the two medical crewmembers had minor injuries; the pilot was unhurt. An examination of the wreckage after the accident did not reveal evidence of a mechanical malfunction or anomaly that would have precluded normal operation. No crew alerting system (CAS) messages were received before impact, and the engine continued to operate after the helicopter came to a rest.
NTSB:20240920195147.s: A helicopter pilot and two medical crewmembers crashed at night while approaching a landing zone. The pilot allowed pitch to increase at low power, causing a rapid descent and hard impact that substantially damaged the aircraft and caused minor injuries to the crew.

NTSB:20240920195148.n: The pilot reported that the airplane likely touched down on the nose landing gear first. The pilot stated that the airplane pitched upward immediately after touchdown, followed by episodes of increasing variation in pitch, then a sudden downward pitch, and the collapse of the nose landing gear. The airplane came to rest on the runway and sustained substantial damage to the engine mount and firewall. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20240920195148.s: The pilot reported the airplane likely touched down on the nose gear first, causing pitch oscillations and subsequent gear collapse. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the engine mount and firewall, with no preaccident mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20240920195153.n: One of the pilots, a flight instructor, was recently hired to instruct in the airplane and was receiving a check out flight from the assistant chief flight instructor. The pilots reported that they were preparing to enter the traffic pattern, so they began a descent from their cruising altitude of about 5,500 ft msl to 1,000 ft msl. About three miles from the airport, both engines on the multi-engine airplane began to run rough. Shortly thereafter, both engines lost all power. Despite the pilots advancing the propellers, mixtures, and throttles to their full forward position, engine power was not restored. The airplane continued to descend, and the pilots performed an off-airport landing onto a field. One of the pilots stated that they did not perform an emergency checklist because there was no checklist for a dual engine failure. Also, due to their proximity to the ground, they did not have time to perform an emergency checklist. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and both wings. A postaccident examination revealed that there were about 25 gallons of fuel in each nacelle, and both fuel selectors were in the "ON" position. The carburetor heat for each engine was in the "OFF" position. Examination of the engines and fuel system did not reveal any mechanical anomalies or failures that would have precluded normal operation. The recorded temperature and dew point near the accident site were conducive to "serious icing" at glide power settings. The pilot operating handbook for the airplane stated that carburetor heat should be used "as required" during approach and landing or if engine roughness occurs. Based on this information, it is likely that carburetor ice formed while the throttles were retarded during the descent which resulted in the initial engine roughness and subsequent loss of engine power due to carburetor ice.
NTSB:20240920195153.s: A flight instructor and assistant chief flight instructor experienced dual engine failure in a multi-engine airplane during descent to the traffic pattern. The probable cause was carburetor ice formation due to carburetor heat being off, resulting in an off-airport landing with substantial damage.

NTSB:20240920195155.n: On September 20, 2024, about 1648 central daylight time, an unregistered Rans S-14 Airaile light sport airplane, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Teague, Texas. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot departed from Teague Municipal Airport (68F) and, shortly afterward, the engine lost power. The airplane was observed to turn back toward the airport apparently in an attempt by the pilot to return for an emergency landing. The airplane subsequently impacted terrain short of the runway. Federal Aviation Administration records revealed that the pilot held a student pilot certificate issued in 2004. At that time, the pilot reported 386 hours total flight experience. The pilot did not hold a current airman medical certificate. However, pilots operating light sport aircraft are not required to hold a medical certificate.
NTSB:20240920195155.s: A student pilot operating an unregistered Rans S-14 Airaile lost engine power shortly after departing Teague Municipal Airport. The pilot attempted a return landing but impacted terrain short of the runway, resulting in substantial aircraft damage and a fatal injury.

NTSB:20240922195157.n: The pilots departed in separate airplanes (a Nanchang CJ-6A and a Yak 52) as a formation flight from the same airport, with the Yak as the lead airplane and the CJ-6A as the dash 2 (wingman) off the Yak’s right wing. According to the Yak pilot, during the flight the pilots briefed their detachment procedure over the radio because they were bound for separate destinations. The briefed procedure was for them to accelerate from 210 kilometers per hour (kph) to 250 kph, at which time the CJ-6A would pitch up and bank left toward the east while the Yak would continue straight. However, during the detachment, and while the Yak pilot looked away briefly to scan his instruments, the CJ-6A entered a slightly inverted and nose-low position above the Yak and the airplanes collided. The Yak’s propeller blades separated and the pilot subsequently made a forced landing on a nearby road, while the CJ-6A rolled right several times and then impacted the ground. Postaccident examination of the CJ-6A and Yak did not reveal any preimpact mechanical anomalies or malfunctions that would have precluded normal operation. The CJ-6A accident site signatures indicated that the airplane impacted the ground in a wings-level and slightly nose-low attitude as most of the energy was absorbed by the lower engine bay. Paint transfer markings and damage signatures from both airplanes indicated that the airplanes collided when the CJ-6A was inverted and canted slightly right of the Yak’s longitudinal axis. The Yak’s propeller impacted the CJ-6A’s left wing and the Yak’s left wing impacted the CJ-6A’s vertical stabilizer, which resulted in a partial separation of the airfoil. There was insufficient evidence to determine either airplane’s final movements prior to the midair collision. The CJ-6A was not equipped with an ejection seat; however, the pilot had a parachute and may have decided to jump from the airplane since the wreckage indicates that the pilot’s canopy was fully open at impact. However, a witness reported that the airplane was in a roll prior to its collision with terrain, so the pilot may not have been able to initiate a jump. Toxicological testing detected the presence of ethanol in the CJ-6A pilot’s cavity blood and gastric contents. Ethanol was not detected in the pilot’s vitreous fluid, which is the preferred specimen type. The other two tested specimen types also contained n-propanol. In the presence of extensive injury, this indicates that the detected ethanol likely was from postmortem sources rather than alcohol consumption. It is unlikely that the CJ-6A pilot was impaired by the effects of ethanol at the time of the accident. The pilots were both part of an association that teaches pilots the fundamentals of formation flight through various clinics. The detachment procedure they used was not in the association’s formation flight manual. In addition, while the Yak pilot reported that they briefed the procedure, there were no recordings to show how the detachment procedure was communicated and whether there were any interpretation errors. The pilot of the CJ-6A did not exhibit any abnormal behavior over the radio or on the ground prior to departure and the flight was not in an area of adverse weather conditions, so it is unknown why the CJ-6A pilot rolled into a nearly inverted position during the detachment. While the accident was initiated by the CJ-6A pilot’s improper roll during the detachment procedure, the Yak pilot failed to continue monitoring the CJ-6A during a critical time as he turned his attention away from the airplane during the detachment.
