The aircraft struck an embankment, sustaining substantial damage to the fuselage and left elevator, with no mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20241015195314.n: The pilot entered the airport traffic pattern on the downwind leg and turned onto the base and final legs for runway 31 with wind from 260° at 5 knots. A witness observed and the pilot reported a normal landing, with the airplane touching down an estimated 300 to 400 ft down the runway. The pilot stated that, during the landing roll, the airplane bounced about 3 ft then touched back down and then, with no brakes applied, the airplane began veering to the left. He attempted to correct with right rudder and right brake but the veer to the left continued and the airplane impacted trees on the left side of the runway. The pilot informed the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airworthiness inspector that he had not noticed any tendencies for the airplane to pull left during landings on previous flights. Postaccident examination of the airplane by a FAA airworthiness inspector revealed substantial damage to the right wing. A check of the flight controls revealed they appeared to be intact and functioning properly. A check of the brakes was performed with no discrepancies noted. A detailed examination of the tail wheel assembly, which was installed in accordance with a supplemental type certificate, revealed it was installed in accordance with the installation requirements, with proper left and right steering springs installed and tensioned. A discrepancy with the tailwheel leaf spring not being centered was noted, but the airplane manufacturer representative reported to the FAA inspector that condition would have negligible effect on taxi operations.
NTSB:20241015195314.s: The pilot landed a tailwheel-equipped airplane on runway 31, but the aircraft bounced and veered left despite rudder and brake inputs, impacting trees. Post-accident inspection found substantial right wing damage and an uncentered tailwheel leaf spring, though the manufacturer stated this had negligible effect on taxi operations.

NTSB:20241015195315.n: The helicopter owner/pilot reported that while he and his flight instructor were practicing an autorotation, the flight instructor heard a noise. Shortly thereafter, the helicopter started to yaw to the left and the airspeed decreased. The flight instructor took over control of the helicopter and initiated an autorotation to a corn field. The right skid caught the ground, and the helicopter rolled onto its right side. The main rotor and fuselage sustained substantial damage. A postaccident examination revealed that the forward tail rotor belt broke. The belt was found frayed at the separation point. A review of the tail rotor maintenance records revealed that the tail rotor belts had not been replaced since 2006. The manufacturer recommends tail rotor belt replacement at 250 hours, 2 years, or as needed upon conditional inspections, whichever comes first. The operator reported that before the accident the belts appeared to be in satisfactory condition but acknowledged they were beyond the 2-year service life and should have been replaced.
NTSB:20241015195315.s: The pilot and flight instructor practicing an autorotation in a helicopter experienced a left yaw and airspeed loss after the forward tail rotor belt broke. The aircraft rolled onto its right side upon landing, sustaining substantial damage due to the belt being frayed and exceeding its two-year service life.

NTSB:20241015195317.n: According to the pilots of the tailwheel-equipped airplane, the pilot/owner offered to let the second pilot land the airplane. During the landing, the airplane landed hard, bounced, and began to yaw to the right. Both pilots then applied control inputs to regain control of the airplane, however the airplane ground looped to the right. Subsequently, the airplane's left main landing gear collapsed, and the left wing impacted the ground, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage and left wing. At the time of the accident, the pilots were landing on runway 14L with wind from 240° at 5 knots. The pilots reported there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20241015195317.s: Pilots of a tailwheel-equipped airplane experienced a hard landing and bounce on runway 14L, leading to a right ground loop. The left main gear collapsed and the left wing struck the ground, causing substantial damage, with no preaccident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20241015195318.n: The pilot of the glider reported that, while on the downwind leg of the airport traffic pattern, he partially deployed the flight spoilers and extended his downwind leg as the glider was too high. He misjudged his distance to the runway during this time and the glider lost more altitude than the pilot had anticipated. The pilot flared during final; however, the glider impacted rough terrain short of the runway threshold. The glider sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the glider that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20241015195318.s: The glider pilot extended the downwind leg by partially deploying spoilers to correct a high approach but misjudged distance, causing excessive altitude loss. The glider impacted rough terrain short of the runway threshold during the flare, sustaining substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage with no mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20241015195319.n: The pilot reported that he was attempting to land a hot air balloon in a field, when the wind shifted. Upon touchdown, one of the passengers exited without the pilot's instruction to do so. As a result of the passenger exiting, the balloon suddenly climbed about 15-20 ft. Subsequently, as the balloon was descending to the ground, the pilot vented out the remaining air from the envelope, which then contacted the ground and a powerline. A spark was observed at the powerline and a small fire ensued, which resulted in substantial damage to the envelope. The pilot reported that the balloon had no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot further stated that a preflight passenger briefing was conducted prior to the flight, which directed passengers to remain in the basket until the pilot gives permission to exit.
NTSB:20241015195319.s: During a hot air balloon landing, a passenger exited the basket without instruction, causing the balloon to climb and subsequently strike a powerline. The resulting spark ignited a fire that caused substantial damage to the envelope, though no mechanical failures were reported.

NTSB:20241015195320.n: The pilot reported that he misjudged the airplane's distance to the runway during the landing flare, and the airplane bounced multiple times. He applied full engine power to abort the landing and retracted the flaps to 10°, but the airplane began to track to the left, and he reduced engine power to idle. The airplane then struck a taxiway sign, and the nose gear struck a concrete culvert. The airplane came to rest in the area between the runway and taxiway and sustained substantial damage to the horizontal stabilizer and lower forward fuselage structure. The pilot reported there were no mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20241015195320.s: The pilot misjudged the landing flare distance, causing multiple bounces and a bounced landing abort. After retracting flaps to 10° and reducing power to idle due to left tracking, the aircraft struck a taxiway sign and culvert, sustaining substantial damage to the horizontal stabilizer and fuselage.

NTSB:20241015195321.n: On October 15, 2024, at 1514 central daylight time, a Rans S12S, N912RS, was involved in an accident near Church Point, Louisiana. The airline transport pilot sustained fatal injuries. The airplane was destroyed. The airplane was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations as a Part 91 maintenance test flight. The airplane had not flown for about three years before it was purchased by the current owner whose intent was to learn how to fly using the accident airplane. The airplane owner, the pilot, and two other individuals performed maintenance on the airplane during the previous two months in preparation for the test flight that was flown by the pilot. During the test flight, the pilot performed maneuvers that included aerodynamic stalls, steep turns, and glide ratios. The pilot reported via radio that there were no issues with the airplane, and it was outstanding in its flying. The pilot then reported that he was returning to the departure airstrip. The airplane entered a downwind landing followed by a base leg for landing. During the turn from the base leg to the final leg of the approach, the airplane snapped over and entered an aerodynamic spin. The airplane descended while spinning and the engine sound increased and then decreased, which was consistent with an application followed by a reduction of engine power. The airplane impacted a field and was destroyed by impact forces. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed no mechanical malfunction/failure that would have precluded normal airplane operation. The airplane was not equipped nor was it required to be equipped with a stall warning system due its experimental categorization.
NTSB:20241015195321.s: An airline transport pilot flying a Rans S12S experimental aircraft on a Part 91 maintenance test flight entered an aerodynamic spin during the base-to-final turn. The aircraft impacted a field and was destroyed, killing the pilot, with no mechanical failure found and no stall warning system installed.

NTSB:20241015195322.n: On August 27, 2024, about 1845 mountain daylight time, a Beech J35, N8350D, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Belgrade, Montana. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, a new pitch trim servo was recently installed as part of the autopilot system update on the airplane prior to the accident flight. The pilot completed a post-maintenance preflight and departed without incident. The pilot started that he conducted a straight-in approach to runway 30 at Bozeman-Yellowstrone International Airport, Bozeman, Montana, about 45-minutes after departure. During the landing flare, he felt the control yoke "jam up" and that it felt as though it "broke free" when he increased aft backpressure on the yoke. The control yoke "jammed up" a second time shortly after the pilot attempted to level the aircraft for landing, and when he applied additional forward movement, the control yoke "broke free" again. Subsequently, the airplane landed hard. A post-accident examination of the airplane revealed that the lower engine mount structure was substantially damage. Additionally, one of the pitch servo bridle cable clamp assemblies (figure 1) appeared to be binding on bulkhead assembly, station 179, a control cable tunnel guide. Figure 1. View of bridle cable clamp slightly aft of the bulkhead assembly at station 179. The airplane was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20241015195322.s: The pilot of a Beech J35 experienced control yoke binding during the landing flare at Bozeman, Montana, following a recent pitch trim servo installation. The aircraft landed hard and sustained substantial damage to the engine mount after the servo bridle cable clamp assembly was found binding on a bulkhead assembly.

NTSB:20241016195324.n: The pilot was conducting a personal cross-country flight. The preflight inspection, engine runup, and takeoff were all normal; however, during the initial climb, just after flap retraction, there was an engine stutter and power reduction followed by "sputtering." The pilot struggled to climb and achieved a maximum altitude of about300 ft above ground level (agl). The pilot performed the engine failure checklist and attempted to troubleshoot but was unsuccessful in restoring engine power. As the stall warning horn sounded, he pushed the nose over and attempted a forced landing on a nearby agricultural field. During the landing flare, the airplane's left wing impacted a hay bale and the airplane veered to the left and rolled down a sloped portion of the field. It then traveled down an embankment, crossed a road, and impacted telephone pole guy wires, separating the left wing before coming to rest. Postaccident examination revealed no evidence of mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane or engine. A maintenance logbook review did not reveal any repetitive or anomalous activity that would result in a loss of engine power. Based on the reported weather conditions at the time of the partial power loss, the airplane was operating in conditions conducive to the formation of serious carburetor icing at glide power and on the boundary of icing at glide and cruise power. Based on this information, it is likely that carburetor icing formed during the 8-minute engine start and taxi before takeoff and the carburetor icing check before takeoff was likely insufficient to melt the ice formed within the carburetor. The pilot reported that he applied carburetor heat after the loss of power, but it was likely insufficient to melt the ice during the short flight.
NTSB:20241016195324.s: During the initial climb of a personal cross-country flight, the pilot experienced engine power loss likely caused by carburetor icing. The pilot attempted a forced landing in a field, but the aircraft struck a hay bale and telephone wires, resulting in a left wing separation.

NTSB:20241016195326.n: The pilot/owner stated that he checked the winds when he was more than 15 miles from the destination airport and again while established on the downwind leg of the traffic pattern. He said the automated weather observing system (AWOS) reported the winds were from 020°at 9 knots "with no gusts" and that he was landing on Runway 03. When over the runway threshold, the nose dropped "due to a decrease in headwind" so the pilot initiated a go-around. After applying "full" engine power and while configuring the airplane for the go-around, an "extreme perpendicular crosswind from the west blew the airplane into the path of trees lining the runway." The pilot said he pulled back on the yoke to clear the trees, the right wing stalled, and the airplane landed hard in a flat attitude resulting in substantial damage and igniting a fire in the engine compartment. Three of the four occupants egressed the airplane with minor injuries while one occupant emerged uninjured. The pilot reported there were no preimpact anomalies or failures that would have precluded normal operation of the airplane. Examination of the AWOS information reported at the airport 15 minutes before arrival revealed winds from 020° at 11 knots gusting to 19 knots. At the time of the accident, winds were reported to be from 040° at 12 knots gusting to 19 knots.
NTSB:20241016195326.s: The pilot/owner of a single-engine airplane initiated a go-around during landing due to a headwind decrease but encountered an extreme crosswind that blew the aircraft into trees. The resulting stall and hard landing caused substantial damage and an engine fire, with all four occupants sustaining minor or no injuries.

NTSB:20241016195327.n: The pilot of the tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that while conducting a wheel landing on a dry lakebed, the airplane veered to the right. Subsequently, the airplane ground looped to the right, the left wing impacted the ground, and the airplane nosed over, coming to rest inverted. As a result, the airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing and empennage. The pilot stated he was unsure why the airplane swerved, adding that it could have been the result of the passenger unintentionally bracing their foot against the right rudder pedal. The pilot also stated the swerve could have been the result of the right wheel brake locking; however, after he had egressed the airplane, he was able to spin the right wheel by hand without any binding noted. Additionally, during the airplane's recovery and transportation, the airplane was able to be rolled on its main wheels with no instances of either main wheel brake locking or seizing.
NTSB:20241016195327.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane ground looped right and nosed over inverted during a wheel landing on a dry lakebed, sustaining substantial damage. The pilot suspected the passenger bracing a foot on the rudder or a locked brake, though post-accident checks found no brake binding.

NTSB:20241016195328.n: The pilot of the tail wheel equipped airplane reported that, during takeoff in a left crosswind, as the tail came up the pilot applied right rudder, but the airplane veered left. After the airplane lifted off the runway the pilot banked left to avoid a windmill in his flight path; however, the tailwheel struck a stock tank. The pilot immediately cut the engine power and the airplane touched down in a left slip folding the left main landing gear under the airplane, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and horizontal stabilizer. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20241016195328.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane veered left during takeoff in a crosswind despite applying right rudder. After striking a stock tank with the tailwheel, the aircraft landed in a left slip, folding the left main gear and causing substantial damage to the wing and stabilizer.

NTSB:20241017195330.n: The pilot reported that while on approach he extended the landing gear, and the three green landing gear indication lights were illuminated; however, he noted that the gear took longer to extend than expected. There was a minimal crosswind, the wind was not gusting, and he lowered the right wing into the crosswind. Upon touch down, the right wing dropped and contacted the runway then the nose gear collapsed, and the gear warning horn sounded. The airplane continued off the right side of the runway and came to rest upright in the grass. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and right wing spar. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the left torque arm for right gear and nose gear was broken. The nose gear push pull rod and rod end for the right gear push pull cable was detached from the left torque arm. The right torque arm for the left gear was intact. The rod end for the left gear push pull cable was still attached and functional.
NTSB:20241017195330.s: During approach, the pilot extended landing gear that took longer than expected to deploy. Upon touchdown, the right wing contacted the runway and the nose gear collapsed due to a broken left torque arm, causing the aircraft to veer off the runway with substantial damage.

NTSB:20241017195331.n: The pilot reported that he was receiving flight instruction and was practicing an instrument approach while utilizing a view-limiting device. The pilot and flight instructor stated that while on final approach, the landing gear lever was lowered. The pilot could not see if the landing gear was extended but he did verify that the green landing gear indicating light was illuminated; then asked the flight instructor to verify that the landing gear was extended. The flight instructor stated that due to the single landing gear indicating light and the brightness of the conditions outside, he could not tell if the landing gear was extended or not. He assumed the landing gear was down because of the increased drag on the airplane. Upon landing, the airplane scraped along the runway and smoke came into the cockpit. The airplane came to rest upright on the runway, and the pilot and flight instructor exited through the door without further incident. The flight instructor said that after the accident the landing gear handle was in the down position and the landing gear circuit breaker was popped. Postaccident examination revealed substantial damage to the lower fuselage. The landing gear circuit breaker was reset, and the landing gear was raised and lowered without issue. The circuit breaker did not trip again during the examination. The landing gear up warning horn did not sound when tested by reducing the manifold pressure below 12 inches. Instead, a landing gear indicating light flashed. The airplane owner said that the landing gear warning horn was not working when he purchased the airplane, and the light was the only indicator to signal that the landing gear was not down. Maintenance records indicated that an annual inspection was complete in September 2024; the landing gear was tested and found to be operating properly during the inspection.
NTSB:20241017195331.s: A student pilot and flight instructor practicing an instrument approach landed with the gear up after relying on a single green indicator light and drag, as the warning horn was inoperative. The aircraft scraped the runway, sustaining substantial lower fuselage damage, though both occupants exited safely.

NTSB:20241017195334.n: During approach to land with the autopilot engaged, in visual meteorological conditions, the airplane struck an object while at a height of about 1,540 ft above the ground, and at a speed of about 170 knots, as the airplane began a left turn toward the final approach course. Just prior to the strike, the pilot briefly saw a white object through the right (copilot side) windscreen, which he initially surmised was a bird. He described the impact as an “extremely loud” booming noise and was like hitting a “Mack truck”. He checked the windscreen for damage and confirmed that the airframe parachute system had not deployed. The airplane’s Emergency Autoland (EA) system had activated, likely due to the collision, and he overheard repeating automated emergency radio transmissions in his headset announcing the airplane’s callsign and declaring an emergency (a function of the EA). These transmissions interfered with his communications with the air traffic control tower, and his initial attempts to deactivate the EA system by pressing the autopilot disconnect button (AP DISC) several times, were unsuccessful. He noticed damage to copilot side sun visor, the copilot side oxygen mask had fallen from its stowed position, a fire extinguishing switch was damaged, the cabin pressure dump switch had activated, and the transponder had changed to the emergency code of 7700 (another feature of the EA system). On-board recorded data indicated that the EA system was ultimately deactivated, though the pilot was unsure if or when it had. He reported that he had no difficulty controlling the airplane, which responded to his flight control inputs as well as flap and landing gear selections, when and as expected. He was able to land the airplane without further incident. Postlanding photographs showed white, red, and blue paint transfer marks leading from the lower left edge to the upper center of the right windscreen, which was inconsistent with a bird strike. The object struck was not identified, as explained later below. The airplane’s on-board recorded data indicated that the EA system had activated twice, in succession. The data indicated neither of the autopilot modes that are a prerequisite for an automatic activation of EA were engaged either time, suggesting that the activations were initiated by the manual button in the overhead panel. The first activation occurred nearly simultaneously (within 1 second or less) when the cabin pressure dump system activated, and likely at the same time as the equipment disturbances in and near the overhead panel. This, along with 1) post accident testing of an exemplar EA button revealed that it would activate when subjected to shock and 2) the pilot’s testimony that he never pressed the EA button, suggests that the first EA activation was most likely due to a shock load to the button during the object strike. However, the on-board recording system did not detect a signal from the button at that time. This was likely due to the recorder’s 1 second sample rate for the EA button status. The EA button (as well as the AP DISC button) is a spring-loaded momentary contact type, which does not remain pressed or latched when pushed. A brief actuation of either of these buttons, shorter than 1 second, may not be detected by the recording system. About 10 seconds after the first EA activation, the recording system detected a signal from the AP DISC button for a single recoding sample. However, the EA did not deactivate. Post incident research and testing by the airframe manufacturer using exemplar avionics revealed two repeatable software defects related to the AP DISC button function. First, the AP DISC button had no effect if pressed during a certain unquantified period of time between about 8-10 seconds after the start of an EA activation. This may explain why the EA system did not deactivate in response to the (single) recorded AP DISC button press. The AP DISC button status was also recorded at a 1 second sample rate. Had the pilot pressed the AP DISC button more than once during the ‘defect’ period, it would likely not have deactivated EA. Further, multiple brief presses of the AP DISC button could have occurred and not been recorded due to the 1 second sample rate. Second, the aural autopilot disconnect warning tone, which is normally sounded through the airplane’s audio system whenever the autopilot is disconnected, would not sound if the AP DISC button was pressed at any time while EA was active. The on-board recorded data indicated that first EA activation was terminated about 20 seconds after it began. This may have been in response to a press of the AP DISC button by the pilot, but if so, the press must have been too brief and between recording samples, as none were recorded. The second EA activation began about 3 seconds after the first one was terminated. At that time, the recoded data captured a signal from the EA button, indicating it had activated. Examination of the EA button assembly did not reveal any obvious damage, though the button was found to be “slightly loose” compared to an exemplar unit. As noted above, an exemplar button was found to be susceptible to activation when shocked, however no apparent source of shock was identified at the time of the 2nd activation. The pilot was adamant in his interview that he did not press the button at any time. The investigation was unable to determine what led to the 2nd button activation. This EA activation was terminated about 20 seconds after it began, and the recording system did not detect a press of the AP DISC button. As noted above, it is possible for brief press of the AP DISC button to not be recorded, however this could not be confirmed. The investigation was unable to identify the object that collided with the incident airplane. The potential for collision with an unmanned aircraft system (e.g. drone, model aircraft) or an experimental balloon were considered. The strike occurred about 30 seconds after the airplane passed by a hobbyist remote control model aircraft field, which was an FAA approved location for unmanned aircraft system (UAS) operations. At the time of the strike, the airplane was 1.8 nm northwest of the model aircraft field, at an altitude of 1,540 ft above the ground. This was well outside the field’s lateral dimensions, and about 1,140 ft above its 400 ft altitude restriction. Given the lateral distance from the model aircraft field, it is unlikely that a remote pilot located at the model aircraft field was operating a UAS flying at the location of the strike, with direct visual observation of the UAS (by either a remote pilot or a visual observer), as required by the FAA and the model aircraft club operating rules. The safety officer for the model aircraft field reported that a polling of club members revealed no known conflicts with the incident airplane. Whether or not a UAS was being operated from the model aircraft field or from any other location, either without direct visual observation, or because of a lost radio communication, could not be determined from the available evidence. While the FAA requires that some UAS be operated with a remote identification (RID) system, a representative from the FAA reported that: there are no archived flights of drones or RID broadcasts remote pilots do not file flight plans Drones are not equipped with radar transponders neither drones nor RID message elements appear on air traffic control radar displays The Civil Air Patrol, which had previously launched some experimental balloons from various locations in and around Austin, reported that they had not conducted any launches on the day of the incident.
NTSB:20241017195334.s: During approach, a pilot reported striking an unidentified object at 1,540 ft, which likely shock-activated the Emergency Autoland system due to a software defect preventing autopilot disconnect. The pilot landed safely, though the object remained unidentified despite proximity to a model aircraft field.

NTSB:20241017195336.n: The pilot reported that the flight was routine until landing, when for some reason he neglected to lower the landing gear. The airplane landed on the runway wheels up and sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot stated there were no mechanical failures or malfunctions associated with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. He added that minimizing distractions and complacency might have prevented the accident.
NTSB:20241017195336.s: The pilot landed the aircraft wheels up during the landing phase, causing substantial fuselage damage. He reported no mechanical failures and attributed the accident to neglecting to lower the gear due to distractions and complacency.

NTSB:20241017195337.n: The pilot and two passengers completed an uneventful flight and refueled the airplane. They departed again, and while established in cruise flight, the engine gradually lost power. The pilot's troubleshooting attempts were unsuccessful in restoring engine power, and the pilot performed a forced landing, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. Postaccident examination revealed that the air induction hose (scat duct) to the fuel servo was the incorrect part and was also damaged and degraded. The scat duct had several tears on the outside that were covered with orange sealant. The sealant was torn open in several places but appeared to have been previously covering tears in the scat duct. The scat duct's internal metal wire was loose and had been rubbing/chafing on the inside of the airbox. The scat duct was able to collapse easily when light pressure was applied to the outside; the internal wiring shifted easily and allowed the scat duct to collapse. The collapsed duct would have restricted airflow to the engine and resulted in a loss of engine power. During an annual inspection about 7 months before the accident, the lower cowl induction air scoop was rebonded to the engine cowling. The failed scat duct would have likely been removed and reinstalled to the airbox during this work, and the mechanic would have been able to assess its condition and recognize that it was not a manufacturer-approved part. The airplane's maintenance logbooks did not document when the scat duct was originally installed or subsequently repaired.
NTSB:20241017195337.s: The pilot and two passengers experienced an engine power loss in cruise due to a collapsed, non-approved air induction hose, forcing a landing that damaged the wing and fuselage. The hose had been previously repaired with sealant and likely mishandled during a maintenance visit seven months prior.

NTSB:20241019195345.n: The pilot was approaching the destination airport following a short cross-country flight when he became incapacitated. The passenger reported that the pilot became unresponsive to her calling out to him. The passenger, who had no prior flight experience, reported that the pilot had already announced his intention to land on the airport's common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF) and that she could see the airport when she took control of the airplane. Witnesses reported that she transmitted "emergency, emergency" on the CTAF. Although other pilots responded and offered assistance, she made no additional transmissions. FAA flight track data showed that after overflying the airport, the passenger made three unsuccessful landing attempts before landing on runway 5 on the fourth attempt. The last flight track data point showed the airplane about 250 ft southwest of the runway 05 threshold on a northeasterly track at a ground speed of 108 knots. The airplane impacted the runway nose first, collapsing the nose landing gear, and slid along the runway. A small fire subsequently developed near the forward portion of the airplane, and the lower forward fuselage sustained substantial damage. The pilot was transported to a local hospital, where he died two days later. Based on the available medical evidence, the pilot's sudden incapacitation was likely due to in-flight cardiac arrest. The pilot had significant underlying heart disease, including coronary artery disease and heart damage from a previous heart attack. Toxicological testing identified no impairing substances. An autopsy was not performed. FAA records showed that the pilot had met the applicable BasicMed requirements for the flight.
NTSB:20241019195345.s: The pilot suffered a cardiac arrest during the approach phase, causing sudden incapacitation. An inexperienced passenger took control, made four landing attempts, and crashed the aircraft on runway 05, resulting in substantial damage and the pilot's subsequent death.

NTSB:20241020195348.n: The pilot was conducting aerobatic maneuvers over desert terrain during an airshow. About 5 minutes into the routine, video evidence showed that the airplane completed two forward tumbles followed by a third tumble that paused briefly while inverted. The airplane then entered a near-vertical descent. In an apparent attempt to recover toward show center, the pilot initiated a high-positive-G pull-up. As the recovery progressed, the right wing appeared to enter an accelerated stall. The airplane subsequently impacted the ground in a nose-low, right-rolling attitude and was destroyed. Examination revealed no anomalies with the airframe or engine that would have precluded normal operation, and damage signatures and witness accounts indicated that the engine was producing power at the time of the accident. The density altitude at the time of the accident was 6,554 ft above mean sea level (msl). The pilot’s shallow upline entry angle into the maneuver, which was less than 45° from level flight and below the pilot’s customary entry profile based on a review of his previous performances of the same maneuver, provided less altitude and energy at the start of the maneuver. Additionally, the pilot initiated the maneuver from an orientation that directed energy toward the ground; initiating the maneuver in the opposite direction would have resulted in an upward energy vector. Subsequent maneuver execution further degraded the airplane’s energy state and available control authority. The pilot’s control inputs during the final portion of the maneuver resulted in an inverted flat spin that culminated in an accelerated aerodynamic stall. A higher entry altitude would have provided additional recovery margin and may have better accommodated the reduction in performance associated with the prevailing high density altitude conditions. The pilot’s initiation of the tumble maneuver at an insufficient altitude with a downward energy vector, combined with the elevated density altitude and pilot’s control inputs, resulted in a loss of energy that culminated in an unrecoverable low-altitude stall.
NTSB:20241020195348.s: During an airshow aerobatic routine, a pilot lost control of the aircraft while performing tumbles at high density altitude. The accident resulted from an insufficient entry altitude and downward energy vector, which led to an unrecoverable low-altitude stall and ground impact.

NTSB:20241021195349.n: The pilot of the commercial air tour helicopter was conducting a night sightseeing flight under visual meteorological conditions. Shortly after departure, the pilot established communication with the Houston Hobby Airport air traffic control tower local controller and requested the “downtown loop.” The local controller identified the helicopter on radar, approved the request, and issued the current altimeter setting. Several minutes later, the controller issued a traffic advisory for another company air tour helicopter. The accident pilot reported that she observed the traffic on her ADS-B display but had not visually acquired it. The controller instructed the accident pilot to maintain visual separation from the traffic, and the pilot was reading back the instruction when her transmission abruptly ended. The helicopter then struck a 1,003-ft-tall radio tower about 100 ft below its top. The air traffic control operations supervisor looked out the air traffic control tower window and witnessed the accident. Video and photographic evidence showed that the tower’s middle and top flashing beacons were operational at the time of the accident; the lower beacon was not visible in any available imagery. The radio tower was depicted as an obstruction on applicable aeronautical charts and on the air traffic controller’s radar display. Flight data showed that the helicopter maintained a straight flightpath toward the tower at an altitude below the top of the tower until impact. An FAA safety review found that traffic volume at the time of the accident was light, with routine complexity, and identified no unusual factors that would have distracted the controller. FAA Order 7110.65, “Air Traffic Control,” paragraph 2-1-2, “Duty Priority,” requires controllers to give first priority to separating aircraft and issuing required safety alerts. Further, FAA Order 7110.65, paragraph 2-1-6, “Safety Alert,” requires a controller to issue a safety alert when the controller is aware that an aircraft is at an altitude that, in the controller’s judgement, places it in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions, or other aircraft. The order further notes that “while a controller cannot see immediately the development of every situation where a safety alert must be issued, the controller must remain vigilant for such situations and issue a safety alert when the situation is recognized.” Although the pilot remained responsible for maintaining clearance from terrain and obstructions while operating under visual flight rules, air traffic control (ATC) safety alert requirements applied once the controller was aware that an aircraft was at an altitude that, in the controller’s judgment, placed it in unsafe proximity to an obstruction. The tower was depicted as an obstruction on the controller’s radar display, and the helicopter’s flight track proceeded toward the tower at an altitude below its top. Traffic volume was light, the controller’s workload was routine, and the FAA safety review identified no unusual factors that would have prevented the controller from monitoring the helicopter’s flightpath. Nevertheless, the controller did not issue a safety alert before the helicopter struck the tower.
NTSB:20241021195349.s: A commercial air tour helicopter pilot struck a 1,003-ft radio tower during a night sightseeing flight after ATC issued a traffic advisory but failed to issue a required safety alert. The controller observed the helicopter on radar approaching the obstruction at an unsafe altitude but did not intervene before impact.

NTSB:20241021195350.n: On October 20, 2024, about 1600 eastern daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Lancair 360, N510G, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident in Cross City, Florida. The commercial pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot had filed an instrument flight rules flight plan from Atmore Municipal Airport (0R1), Atmore, Alabama to Cross City Airport (CTY), Cross City, Florida. The pilot reported in his flight plan an estimated time enroute time of 2 hours, and that there were 4 hours of fuel aboard the airplane. Review of preliminary Federal Aviation Administration Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) data revealed that the airplane departed 0R1 about 1430. At 1520, while in contact with Tallahassee approach control, the airplane’s ADS-B track and radio contact with the pilot were lost. The air traffic controllers made multiple attempts to re-establish communication including identifying turns, instructions to “squawk IDENT,” and transmitting on the VHF emergency frequency, with no response from the accident airplane. As the airplane left the Tallahassee approach control area it was handed off to Jacksonville Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC), who also attempted to contact the pilot with no response. Jacksonville ARTCC continued to track the airplane as a primary radar target until radar contact was lost about 24 miles from CTY. Another pilot, who was flying into CTY about the time of the accident, reported that he heard the accident airplane make a radio transmission on the CTY common traffic advisory frequency. The accident pilot stated there had been an electrical failure, that he was transmitting with a handheld radio, and that he was requesting a “gear check” while on the downwind leg of the traffic pattern for runway 4. After hearing no response from anyone on the ground, the other pilot reported that he offered to check the accident airplane’s landing gear, but he received no response. A short time later he heard an emergency locator transmitter broadcasting on the VHF emergency frequency and saw debris as he overflew CTY. A witness, who lived near CTY and heard the airplane as it flew overhead, described that the engine sounded like it was “spitting, sputtering, and backfiring through the exhaust.” An eyewitness on the ground reported that the airplane overflew the fixed base operator building at CTY at an altitude of about 600 to 700 ft. He described that the airplane’s engine sounded like it was “missing.” He added that as the airplane overflew the airport, it began a left descending turn. About 100 ft above the ground, the left wing and nose of the airplane dropped suddenly, and the airplane impacted the ground. The airplane came to rest on the airport property, about 4,500 ft from the runway 4 threshold, and 210 ft right of the runway 4 centerline, between runway 4 and taxiway Bravo. The debris path was about 160 ft in length and was oriented on a magnetic heading of 048°. All major components of the airplane were discovered along the debris path. The initial ground impact scar was about 100 ft from the main wreckage site and green lens glass was observed in the scar. The main wreckage was oriented on a magnetic heading of 340°. The outboard section of the right wing was observed about 60 ft past the main wreckage and was the last piece of debris observed. Control continuity was confirmed from the left aileron, elevator, and rudder flight control surfaces to the flight controls in the cockpit. The right aileron remained attached to the right wing section, which was impact-separated from the fuselage. Control continuity of the right aileron could not be confirmed due to impact damage. The flap drive motor and worm gear were not extended, which corresponded to the flaps being in an “up” position. The landing gear position selector was found in the “retract” position. Fuel was found throughout the airframe fuel system, in both wing fuel tank boost pumps and filters, in the header tank boost pump and filter, and in the fuel strainer. The header fuel tank and both wing fuel tanks were breached during the impact sequence, and each contained no residual fuel. No evidence of fuel smell or vegetation blight was observed at the accident site. The airplane was equipped with two engine-driven alternators. One belt-driven alternator was installed to the front of the engine, and remained attached. The drive belt for the alternator remained attached to the alternator pully and was intact. The second alternator was installed on the engine’s accessory case and was directly driven from the engine’s accessory section. The main 12-volt battery remained attached to the fuselage, and when measured with a multimeter, about 11.8 volts were observed. A second 12-volt battery was impact separated and found in the wreckage debris path. When measured with a multimeter, about 12.5 volts were observed. The engine remained partially attached to the fuselage through the tubular mount and was upside down at the accident site. Thumb compression and suction were confirmed during postaccident examination of the engine. Crankshaft and valvetrain continuity were confirmed through multiple rotations of the crankshaft. The engine was equipped with two E-Mag electronic ignition systems. Oil was present in the oil sump and the oil filter was impact-separated from the engine. Fuel was observed in the engine-driven fuel pump, fuel servo, and the fuel flow divider. A fuel receipt was discovered in the wreckage indicating the pilot had purchased 15.69 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel the morning of October 20 at Jasper County Airport – Bell Field (JAS), Jasper, Texas. Another receipt from 0R1 showed that the pilot had purchased 24.13 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel at 1313. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20241021195350.s: A commercial pilot and passenger were fatally injured when their experimental Lancair 360 crashed near Cross City, Florida, after losing radio contact and experiencing engine issues. The pilot reported an electrical failure and requested a gear check before the aircraft entered a descending turn and impacted the ground with the landing gear retracted.

NTSB:20241021195351.n: While conducting a post-flight walkaround inspection, the pilot discovered two through penetrations of the ventral vertical stabilizer and damage to three propellor blade leading edges, likely from foreign object debris. The stabilizer sustained substantial damage. The source of the debris could not be determined. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. This airplane is an exported former Beechcraft Starship 2000A that was issued a new special airworthiness certificate as an experimental Enterprise during import.
NTSB:20241021195351.s: During a post-flight walkaround, the pilot discovered two through penetrations on the ventral vertical stabilizer and damage to three propeller blade leading edges on an experimental Enterprise aircraft. The damage was likely caused by foreign object debris, though the source remained undetermined.

NTSB:20241021195354.n: The pilot reported that during a go-around after a bounced landing, the engine did not produce full power. The pilot chose to perform the go-around due to the bounced landing on the short, grass runway. During engine throttle application, the pilot noticed that the airplane did not attain the normal acceleration rate. The pilot verified the position of the cockpit engine controls; however, the airplane was still underperforming. Before the pilot could attempt any further actions, the airplane settled into the tree line at the end of the runway, impacted multiple trees, and came to rest inverted about 4 feet off the ground, which resulted in substantial damage to both wings, the fuselage, and the empennage. Multiple witnesses reported that the engine sounded as if it was not producing full rated power. Postaccident examination of the airframe revealed no evidence of mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. However, a review of recorded engine data showed that the engine was not producing full power during the approach, landing, and go-around. Recorded engine monitor data indicated a sharp drop in the No. 1 cylinder’s Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) from 1321° F to 365° F as the pilot was turning onto final approach. Over the next minute, the No. 1 cylinder’s EGT rebounded twice before again falling relative to the other cylinders’ EGTs. When the pilot applied full engine power during the go-around, the No. 1 cylinder’s EGT jumped from 532° F to 863° F for less than one second before again dropping down to 526° F. Three seconds later the No. 1 cylinder’s EGT returned to normal, in line with the other cylinders; however, full engine power was not restored until 11 seconds after the pilot commanded full engine power. This is likely the No. 1 cylinder air fuel mixture was too lean for proper combustion. At the start of the initial decent, the highest recorded cylinder EGT temperature was 1,467° F and the lowest 1,306° F. At the start of the descent from traffic pattern altitude for landing, the highest recorded cylinder EGT was 1,480° and the lowest was 1,351° F. During the go-around, the fuel flow was steady at about 10 gph until the end of the recording when the fuel flow suddenly increased to 15 gph in about one second. Additional review of the engine data revealed that during takeoff and initial climb, the maximum recorded fuel flow was 20.6 gph which is 2.4 gallons below the minimum required full engine power fuel flow of 23.0 gph. Review of the maintenance logbooks did not reveal a fuel injection system calibration during the most recent annual inspection as required by manufacturer’s maintenance manual. Due to a lack of recent calibration of the fuel injector system, it is likely that the system would not have provided the required fuel flow to the engine. On the accident flight, the pilot likely did not enrichen the mixture before starting the descent until after established in the go-around. During the go-around, the pilot likely observed that the mixture was not properly set when he noticed the degraded performance of the engine. This is consistent with the sudden increase in recorded fuel flow and engine power before end of the data and subsequent impact with trees.
NTSB:20241021195354.s: The pilot attempted a go-around on a short grass runway after a bounced landing, but the engine failed to produce full power due to a lean mixture caused by uncalibrated fuel injectors. The aircraft struck trees and came to rest inverted with substantial damage before power was restored.

NTSB:20241021195355.n: On October 19, 2024, at 1450 pacific daylight time (PDT), a Diamond DA40, N895AM, and a Boeing 737-7H4, N250WN, operated as SWA1671, were involved in a runway incursion in Long Beach, CA. There were no injuries reported and none of the aircraft were damaged. N895AM was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight and had departed Camarillo Airport (CMA) with a destination of Long Beach Airport, Daugherty Field (LGB). SWA1671 was operated as a Title 14 CFR Part 121 passenger flight and had departed San Francisco Bay Oakland International Airport (OAK) with a destination of LGB. A review of Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) air traffic control (ATC) audio recordings indicated that at 1442:36 PDT, the crew of N895AM established communication with the local control one (LC1) controller and reported inbound on the Area Navigation (RNAV) Runway 30 Zulu approach. The LC1 controller cleared N895AM to land on runway 30 and instructed the crew to hold short of runway 26 right for traffic. The crew of N895AM then requested to circle to land on runway 26 right which the LC1 controller verbally confirmed with the crew. At 1444:38, the LC1 controller denied the circling request and again cleared N895AM to land on runway 30 and hold short of runway 26 right for traffic. The crew acknowledged with an accurate read back. At 1446:46, the crew of SWA1671 established communication with the LC1 controller and reported inbound for landing on runway 30. At 1447:20 the LC1 controller cleared SWA1671 to land on runway 30 and provided a traffic advisory to the crew reference an uninvolved aircraft in the pattern. The crew acknowledged with an accurate readback. At 1448:27, the LC1 controller provided a traffic advisory to the crew of SWA1671 reference a Cessna that was landing runway 26 left. At 1449:50, the crew of N895AM advised the LC1 controller they were holding short of runway 26 right on runway 30. At 1450:05, as SWA1671 was completing their landing roll out on runway 30, the crew of SWA1671 advised the LC1 controller that there was an aircraft on runway 30. Following the runway incursion, both aircraft taxied to their requested parking areas without further incident. Figure 1 shows the ground tracks of N895AM (indicated by the blue track) and SWA1671 (indicated by the yellow track) overlaid on satellite imagery in Google Earth. The illustration depicts the direction of travel for each airplane as well as their closest estimated proximity. Figure 1. Overhead view of the flight tracks of N895AM and SWA1671 with the area of closest proximity. Upon notification, an NTSB Air Traffic Control (ATC) working group was formed. Parties to the investigation include the FAA and the National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA). Certified Automatic Dependent Surveillance – Broadcast (ADS-B) data and audio recordings were provided by the FAA and were used in constructing this preliminary report. The NTSB is currently analyzing this data. During the week of October 28th, 2024, the ATC working group convened at Long Beach Airport Traffic Control Tower (LGB ATCT), the facility that was providing services to both airplanes at the time of the incident, and conducted interviews with the LC1 and LC2 controllers, and operations supervisor who were working at the time of the incident, as well as the NATCA Vice Facility Representative and Air Traffic Manager.
